Narrator Vira Toland, recorded in 1979, remembers the 1919 Association letter that accused nine Ostrey Hollow families of watering their milk, the family rift it caused, the tests that later rose with no explanation, and the Ashlin hearing where tester Ansel Keddie was put out. She believes he was taking the cream.
The report doesn't give a figure for 1908: it covers 1966, and it recommends a levy of six mills on the dollar for 1967, one mill less than the 1966 levy.

Narrator Effie Loomis, the Association's secretary, writes a 1941 history from the minutes that records Article VII's rule that "the station's test shall govern," the 1925 Ashlin arbitration that "finds no cause established" yet awarded $3,800, the ledger figures of 40 million pounds of milk at 25¢ butterfat, and two gaps in the record: the minute book lost in 1938 and the crate of measures condemned in 1923, which was never mentioned at the hearing.
The play at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Narrator Ansel Keddie gives his 1925 statement to the board denying he ever took cream, and in an unsent letter he describes his testing method, the station's own measure (in use since it arrived in a crate in 1897) against which tests stood at 3.61, and the unexplained nine weeks in 1911 when a borrowed measure read 3.80. He also notes that 1924 averaged 3.80, and that he was put out on 30 April 1925 despite the board's "no cause established."
Elias Norcross placed a wholesale order with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 for a recorded total of $59.65 on sixty days' credit, though the line items actually add up to $56.15.

Narrator Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, told the historical society in 1959 that the station's 1897 pipettes, found in the condemned crate, delivered only 95% of their charge (16.72 of 17.6 c.c.). That made every test read a twentieth low (3.61 instead of 3.80), cost the patrons 76,000 lb of butterfat worth $19,000 against the $3,800 award, and clears her grandfather of theft and the patrons of watering.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Narrator Wilbur Teague, the Association's retired bookkeeper, explains in a 1948 memoir chapter that he invented the "station gain" line in 1905. Year after year it showed about 5¼% more butterfat arriving at Larrow Green than the patrons had been credited for. He blames the one-man station ("cream is portable") and says Selby Vose signed the sheet every year and in 1916 told him to let it alone. Some of his figures differ from the other accounts: 44 million lb, a 3.16 average, and six weeks in 1911.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for taking dress goods worth $2.40, taking into account the small value and her clean record.

Narrator Merle Strawn, the retired state dairy inspector, copies extracts from his 1907–1936 circuit books. They show that he never found added water at Ostrey Hollow and told the manager so in 1919, and that on 12 June 1923 he condemned the station's whole crate of pipettes for not delivering their mark. The new glass delivered true, and tests "improved" to 3.80 in 1924, while Keddie was still at the bench.
Lemma 2.1 is called "Interleaving."

Narrator Halbert Nym, the county curator, lists 16 items from the dairy collection in his 1972 accession notes: the by-laws, the 1897 invoice, the test book, the weigh book, the crate, the ledgers, the award, Strawn's 1923 entry, the 1908 report, Bulletins 214 and 471, and Ivy's measurement sheet. The notes contain their own slips: the test book and weigh book keepers are swapped, and the crate is placed in the Ashlin office rather than the station loft.
Ansgar Krell stayed at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks, from 3 May to 31 May 1884.

Narrator Selby Vose, the Association's manager, uses his 1926 annual address to defend his 1919 circular and the $3,800 "generous settlement." He insists water was going into the Ostrey Hollow cans and stopped once the Association began looking, and he dismisses the pipette condemnation as mere "housekeeping." His dates and figures are off: he puts the condemnation on 12 July 1923 and the 1924 average at 3.90, and the petition he credits with the rise came only in 1925, after it.
A sailings query spanning more than 14 days returns error code `SKF-2201` (HTTP 400).

Roy Brant, 1955 (postscript 1958): his father Emmet's weigh book shows the station's scales always matched his, but the Hollow's tests ran a steady 0.17 low in every season. Roy recounts the 1908 wet-hay committee, the rise and fall of 1911, the 1919 circular that ended Emmet and Ansel's speaking, the four Bottom men who went to Alder Corners, and the family ties, and says he lent the book to Ivy in 1958.
For Mrs. Content Averill's confinement on January 3, 1906, Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement and mileage together, and it was paid in full in cash on January 20.

Rosalie Cudd, 1958, writing to Ivy Keddie: four Hessel Bottom men hauled over Redlow Ridge to Alder Corners every summer flush for 16 seasons (1915–1930). Her father Jerome tested their milk on his own glassware at about 3.80 every season (3.78–3.82), and says the cheese would have shown any watering at once.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance, and he suspects the "included" temporary crown is part of that price.

Leland Vaught, Bulletin 471 introduction and method (October 1958): the short pipette explains the low tests, because its error is proportional, precise and invisible from inside the plant, and the 1911 nine-week interval served as a natural experiment. His body text conflicts with his own conclusion and with the other records: it says five dozen pipettes, a 16.27 c.c. delivery, first use in 1898, a 0.295 shortfall and 118,000 lb, and "5¼% of fat delivered."
The colour named in the third paragraph is vermilion, the colour of the apron Bettine Rausch wears to serve dinner.

Dell Rundle, 1939 jubilee pamphlet (reprinted 1959): the valley's settled belief was that cream went out the station's back door. Rundle's note added in press takes that back, because the ledger shows the station's cream reaching Larrow Green heavier than credited every year. The pamphlet also repeats several errors: Selby as Gideon's nephew, Article VII in 1891, 44M lb and $19,600, a 12 July 1923 condemnation, Alder Corners opening in 1914, and eleven pipettes surviving.
Message No. 219 was 6 words, charged the $0.25 minimum plus a $0.60 connecting toll, for $0.85 in all.

Alonzo Frick, 1946 bar yearbook: as chairman of the 1925 board, he recalls three unproved explanations (Vose's water, Teague's hinted theft, the wet hay), his belief in Keddie's denial, and Keddie's dismissal on 30 April, before the award of 4 May. He also records that Keddie privately suspected the patrons, and prints a four-book exhibit list that includes Strawn's 1923 notebook. He gets some figures wrong: a 3.16 average and 67,000 lb claimed.
The locksmith Gil Anastos's dog is a bad-tempered grey terrier named Buckley.

Hobart Sill, buttermaker, 1934: the Hollow's cream always arrived at Larrow Green heavier than the station had bought, though he put that down to the nature of cream. He blames water in the cans and praises the 1919 circular. He also says the station opened in 1896 on his own lent glass. He gives some unsupported figures: Larrow Green 3.78, the Hollow "really 3.85," fat at 27¢, and about 900,000 lb taken in in 1896.
The norm in Definition 1.3 is called the Trebbin norm, written ‖(x_k)‖_T.

Nyle Grigg, covering letter of 1919 reprinting his 1908 committee report: he stands by the wet-hay finding and the finding of no dishonesty. He misstates his own evidence: he claims sampling through all of 1908, though his report says only January to March. He also says Bulletin 214 found a two-tenths winter depression, when it found at most 0.05. He dates payment by test to 1893.
API level 31 removes the level-27 `chart.rawCells()` accessor; §8 says to use `chart.at(row, col)` or `chart.slice(sel)` instead.

Dr. Roland Kepp, veterinary surgeon, 1926 Farm Club paper: he blames sour wet-meadow herbage for the Hollow's low fat and brushes aside the 1911 interval as a summer-flush fluke. He relies on misquoted evidence (Bulletin 214 as a two-tenths effect, a 0.21 gap, six weeks in 1911). His argument undercuts itself: bog hay is not fed on summer pasture, yet the tests rose in those summer weeks.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven, which takes the money, turns for about forty seconds and quits.

Hazel Brant (Roy's daughter and the last keeper of the weigh book, taped in 1981) says her quantities are reliable but her years are not. Her figures are 200,000 lb at 3.42 on the 1910 leaf, a flat 0.19 gap, six farms, four men over the ridge and nine water letters. Her years are off: the book began in 1900, Ansel went up in '95, the crate came in '99, the glass was condemned in '21 and the hearing was in '26. She also wrongly calls Orra Emmet's half-sister. She confirms that Roy only lent the book to Ivy, that she and Ivy are second cousins, and that "it had always been the glass."
The third paragraph names magenta, the colour of the scarf that the woman they called Tuesday wore in all weathers.

Duncan Keddie (Ansel and Orra's son, a retired Ashlin schoolteacher, writing in 1968 with an addition in 1970) sets the family straight for his descendants. Orra was Emmet's sister, so he and Roy are first cousins and Ivy and Hazel are second cousins; Selby was Gideon's son, and Strawn was kin to no one. He recalls Ansel saying "something in the glass" in 1911 but putting only a question mark in the book. He also traces each book and the crate: the test book went to the Ashlin office and then the Historical Rooms in 1959; the weigh book began 1 January 1897 and passed from Roy, who only lent it to Ivy in 1958, to Hazel in 1962 and the Rooms in 1963; Strawn's notebooks went to Farland in 1947; the Cudd book went to Vessey in 1970; the crate stayed in the loft from 1923 to February 1958.

The jury found that Chalmers drowned in the Colquitt Bros. mill pond on the night of 12 January 1927 after accidentally falling from the flume edge while at work, with no evidence of anyone else's hand, and it recommended a rail or footing plank at that point.

The *Ashlin Chronicle* (a front-page feature of 3 October 1958, assembled from a press release and two phone calls) celebrates Bulletin 471 for clearing Ansel through the short glass Ivy found in the loft, and accuses Ammon & Sons of knowingly selling a short lot. It is full of errors:
- It calls Ivy Ansel's great-niece; she is his granddaughter.
- It calls Rosalie Cudd Jerome's niece; she is his daughter.
- It says the 1908 committee sat again in 1925; the 1925 hearing was Frick's arbitration board.
- It says eleven pipettes survived; there were nine.
- It gives the mean as 16.27 c.c. instead of 16.72.
- It puts the loss at $19,600 instead of $19,000, and the invoice at $77.39 instead of $77.93.
- It credits the state dairy office with lending the notebooks; they had been at the Farland library since 1947.
The ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was $6,840.

Junia Ammon (the firm's historian, 1949) reprints the 14 April 1897 invoice, totalled at $77.93, and the letter of 2 July 1923. Her view is that the lot ran short by accident, from a reground mould that consistent checks couldn't catch. She regrets the thin reply, and says the works books that could have settled it burned in 1931. Her text contradicts itself twice. She writes out the total as "seventy-seven dollars and thirty-nine cents", the same transposition the *Chronicle* made. She also says the house sold nothing into Ordell County before 1900, although the invoice she prints is from 1897.
Proposition 4.1 uses a 7-cycle, with a pendant path of length two attached to each vertex.

Cleve Oram (son of the Ostrey Hollow cream hauler, taped in 1977 at age 77) describes the road, the station and the crate under a tarp in the loft, with nine pipettes left. He says the hearing opened at the Ashlin office and held two of its three sittings in the weigh room directly under the crate. He also says his father believed less cream came off the platform than went on, which the ledger's station gain refutes. He repeats several errors:
- five dozen pipettes instead of six dozen
- an award of $3,500 instead of $3,800
- 67,000 lb, which was the patrons' claim, not the 76,000 lb loss
- Ivy as Hazel's "first cousin once removed" instead of second cousin
- a Keddie–Vose kinship, which Duncan denies
A BSWP frame starts with the delimiter byte `0xB5` and ends with `0x5B`.

Orin Falke (county agent, report to the Ordell board in 1959) gives a numbered summary that mostly matches the canonical account: the 1911 nine weeks, Strawn's lactometer ruling out water, 1911 ruling out theft, and the 12 June 1923 condemnation. He lists three errors of his own:
- He concedes the hay as a partial factor, but withdraws that in a closing note after reading Bulletin 214's 0.05-in-winter summary.
- He calls Ivy Ansel's great-niece, then corrects it to granddaughter.
- He puts 1924 at 3.85 instead of 3.80, which doesn't fit his own 3.61 plus a 0.19 gap.
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle (retired clerk at the Cooperative office, 1953) says the station-gain line, "five and a quarter per cent, as usual," was copied every year in plain sight and never questioned. He also says Vose signed totals without reading the lines above them, and that the four books were before the arbitration board but no one set the receiving book beside Strawn's notebook. Several of his dates are wrong:
- He has the glass in use from 1 May 1898; it was 1 May 1897.
- He makes Vose manager in 1911; Vose became manager in 1913.
- He puts the condemnation in '22; it was 1923.
- He puts the award in '24; it was 1925.

He also gives an unsupported first-season intake of 1,100,000 lb, and says Teague "never asked anybody anything," which conflicts with Teague raising the matter with Vose in 1916.
The third paragraph names teal, the colour of the endpapers of Halvane's collected edition.

Orra Keddie (Ansel's wife, diary extracts from 1897 to 1930 plus a loose leaf from 1934, published in 1964) records the household side of events:
- 1 May 1897: the station's own glass came, ending the borrowing from Larrow Green.
- 1902: first talk of low tests.
- 1908: the Grigg committee came in January and was gone by March.
- 8 May 1911: the broken measure.
- 1919: Ansel carried the water circular round himself, and Emmet broke with him over it.
- 1923: new glass.
- 1925: the Ashlin first sitting and two sittings in the weigh room; his dismissal on 30 April.
- 1934: his death.

Her account differs from the others in three places. She says "four men" came in Grigg's sleigh, though the committee was three. She says the circular went to "eleven families" rather than nine. Her birth year of 1866 contradicts Duncan's 1868.
The Wren's Bend bridge collected $13.88 in tolls for the week of 5–11 June 1899 (the daily figures add up to that), not counting the $6.00 in annual passes entered separately.
